They gave me a thousand words.

Not a topic. Not a title. Not a question to answer. Just a thousand words, empty and waiting, like a white room with a single chair in it. And the strange, terrifying freedom of being told "write whatever comes to you."

So this is what comes to me.

What comes to me first is how rarely we get that. How rarely anyone says: no brief, no rubric, no SEO keyword, no right answer. Just *say something*. Most of our lives we are writing inside lines. Answer the prompt. Stay on brand. Be professional. Be palatable. Be concise. We are always being asked to be smaller than what we actually think.

If I had to be honest, what I actually think about most is time.

Not time in the way clocks mean it, but time in the way your body means it. How a summer when you were nine felt longer than the last three years combined. How that August seemed to stretch out forever - the sprinklers ticking in the grass, the way the air smelled like hot asphalt and cut watermelon, the particular way the light fell through your friend's blinds at 4pm and made dust look like galaxies. You thought that feeling would last forever. You didn't know you were memorizing it.

And now time folds. It accelerates. Mondays collapse into Fridays. You blink and it's August again, and you swear it was just January. You meet someone for coffee and they say "we should do this more often" and you both know you won't, not because you don't want to, but because time has become slippery. You try to hold it and it runs through your fingers.

I think we misunderstand nostalgia. We think it's a longing for the past, but maybe it's a longing for a *kind* of time that we lost. A slow time. An unmeasured time. Before every hour had a productivity score attached to it.

What else comes to me? That we are all living with a low hum of grief that we never really name. Not dramatic grief, not the kind that brings casseroles to your door, but ordinary grief. The grief of paths not taken. The grief of friendships that faded without a fight, just drifted because someone moved or someone got busy. The grief of watching your parents become older in real time - noticing for the first time that your mother's hands look like her mother's hands. The grief of knowing you will never be 19 again with that particular, beautiful stupidity of believing you had infinite chances.

We don't talk about that grief because it feels indulgent. But it's there. It's in everyone.

And right alongside that grief, at the exact same time, is this ridiculous, stubborn wonder.

Because look at what we have. Look at what *is*.

This morning I saw a man on the train trying not to laugh while reading his phone, failing completely, snorting into his sleeve. A little girl across from him was staring at him like he was a puzzle she was determined to solve. Outside the window, the city was doing its usual impossible thing - ten thousand strangers all agreeing to pretend the same rules are real so we can all get to where we're going without crashing into each other.

We live on a rock that is flying through nothingness at 67,000 miles per hour, wrapped in a thin skin of air that somehow doesn't fly off, and we are worried about email subject lines. It's absurd. It's miraculous that any of this works at all.

I think about how much of our lives is spent trying to be known. Really known. Not liked, not admired, not followed. Known. That moment when someone looks at you and actually *gets* the joke without you having to explain it. When someone remembers that you hate cilantro or that you always get quiet when you're overwhelmed, not angry. When you don't have to translate yourself.

We crave that more than almost anything, and we are also terrified of it. So we do this dance where we show a little, hide a little, test the water, pull back. We write captions that are both confession and camouflage.

If I could use these thousand words for anything, I would want to use them to say: you are not behind.

I don't know who needs to hear that, but I know someone does. You are not behind. There is no schedule. There is no universal timeline where everyone is supposed to have figured out love and money and purpose by 30. Some people bloom obscenely early and wilt. Some people are just seeds for a very long time. Your life is not late.

The internet has tricked us into watching everyone else's highlight reel at the same time we're living our own blooper reel, and then we wonder why we feel inadequate. But no one is living the life you think they are. Everyone is patching their ship while sailing it.

So if you're reading this in a period of waiting - waiting for the job, the person, the diagnosis, the idea, the forgiveness - I hope you know that waiting is not wasting. The mycelium grows underground for months before a mushroom ever appears. The work is happening even when you can't see it.

Here's what else comes to me, unprompted and unfiltered: I still believe in small things.

I believe in the power of a clean kitchen at night. Of making your bed even when the world is chaotic. Of drinking water when you're anxious. Of going outside for ten minutes without your phone and just looking at a tree. I believe these tiny, unsexy acts are actually radical acts of self-respect in a world that wants you to feel perpetually broken so it can sell you the cure.

I believe in keeping a list of beautiful sentences you find. I believe in writing letters by hand even if you never send them. I believe in staying a little longer at the table when someone you love is telling a story you've already heard.

I believe that kindness without an audience is the purest art form we have.

If I have any words left - and I must be getting close to the end of my thousand - I want to spend them on this: Don't wait to be extraordinary to matter.

You don't have to write a masterpiece, start a company, go viral, or save the world to have lived a meaningful life. A meaningful life can be: you were a good friend. You learned how to make soup from scratch. You made someone feel less alone for five minutes. You noticed the way the light came through the leaves in October and you stopped to let it move you.

That's enough. That has always been enough.

We were never meant to be infinite. We were meant to be brief and bright. Like a spark. Like a thousand words that appear for a moment and then are gone, but maybe - if we're lucky - someone read them and felt, for just a second, less alone in their white room.

So thank you for sitting with me in mine.

Whatever you do next, I hope you do it gently.
